subsystems.name: Optical pulse oximeter
subsystems.role: tracks blood-oxygen saturation through the skin, the signal that dips when breathing pauses.

subsystems.name: Motion sensing
subsystems.role: detects body movement and the small surges that mark arousals and breathing effort.

subsystems.name: On-device signal processing
subsystems.role: turns raw optical and motion data into nightly breathing-disturbance features.

subsystems.name: Power system
subsystems.role: keeps the sensors running through a full night without a nightly charge.

subsystems.name: Radio, app and reporting
subsystems.role: moves the nightly result to a phone and presents a risk signal rather than a diagnosis.

buildSteps.title: Define what to measure
buildSteps.detail: Clinical scoring of apnoea uses airflow, breathing effort and oxygen desaturation, summarised as an apnoea–hypopnoea index in events per hour. A wrist device cannot measure airflow directly, so it targets the oxygen dips and movement surges that follow each pause, plus the resulting fragmentation of sleep.

buildSteps.title: Choose and place the sensors
buildSteps.detail: Reflective pulse oximetry shines red and infrared light into the skin and reads what scatters back; placing the emitter and photodiode on the back of the wrist keeps good contact with the skin for most sleep positions. An accelerometer sits on the same board.

buildSteps.title: Gather labelled training data
buildSteps.detail: Volunteers wear the prototype overnight while undergoing attended polysomnography in a sleep laboratory. Each night of wearable data is paired with the technician-scored breathing events, giving thousands of labelled hours across ages, body types, medications and health conditions.

buildSteps.title: Train and test the detection model
buildSteps.detail: The model learns the nightly pattern — repeated 3 % or larger oxygen dips, their clustering, motion arousals — and outputs either a nightly index or a simple risk notification. It is tested on nights and people held out of training, and separately across skin pigmentation, because melanin absorbs the oximeter's light and can bias readings.

buildSteps.title: Engineer the wearable
buildSteps.detail: Sensor, microcontroller, battery and haptics are integrated into a watch-sized case, the optical path is calibrated against a reference oximeter, and the enclosure is sealed so the device can be worn continuously, including in the bath and shower.

buildSteps.title: Validate against a clinical standard
buildSteps.detail: Prospective studies compare the device's nightly output with simultaneous polysomnography or a validated home sleep test. The claim is deliberately narrow: flagging people at moderate-to-severe risk who should be tested, not diagnosing apnoea or distinguishing its causes.

buildSteps.title: Fit the care pathway
buildSteps.detail: A notification routes the wearer to a clinician, who orders a home sleep-apnoea test or a laboratory study. The device only works as a front door to diagnosis; without that pathway, a flag produces anxiety and no treatment.

buildSteps.title: Maintain and iterate
buildSteps.detail: Firmware updates improve artefact rejection, verify the device is being worn properly, and respond to drift in the optical sensor as it ages. Post-market surveillance tracks false negatives and complaints.

prerequisites.why: measuring oxygen saturation from the wrist rather than a fingertip is the core sensing trick.
regulators require agreement studies against the laboratory standard before any screening claim.
sleep-lab data is expensive, skewed towards people who already seek care, and thin in some skin tones and age groups.

prerequisites.tech: Bias-corrected optical sensing across skin tones
prerequisites.why: darker skin can cause oximeters to overestimate saturation, which risks missing real events.

prerequisites.tech: A routing pathway into sleep medicine
prerequisites.why: a flag is only useful if the person can actually reach a test and a clinician.

pathway.milestone: consumer watches and under-mattress sensors flag likely moderate-to-severe sleep apnoea and prompt a doctor visit
pathway.unlocks: screening a population that would otherwise never be tested.

pathway.milestone: larger validation studies across skin tones, ages and conditions, with results published rather than only filed with regulators
pathway.unlocks: trust from sleep physicians and clearer limits on who should not rely on the signal.

pathway.milestone: tighter pairing of wearables with home sleep-apnoea tests
pathway.unlocks: fewer people needing an expensive night in a laboratory to get a diagnosis.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop monitoring linked to therapy, from auto-titrating positive-airway-pressure machines to implanted nerve stimulators
pathway.unlocks: treatment adjusted from nightly data instead of a yearly clinic visit, and better tracking of cardiovascular risk linked to untreated apnoea.
